component_findings.dependency_declaration: Recertified level 3 under the current criterion: Direct dependencies can be declared explicitly at an appropriate project/module boundary rather than inferred from ambient state. Evidence basis: language-level dependency semantics: JDK self-sufficiency for compile/run, JPMS module declarations vs classic classpath ambiguity risk | Java core language plus JDK (javac/java) has zero external native dependencies to build or run a program: 'javac Main.java && java Main' works with only the JDK installed. | Reviewed /quidra-benchmark/template/programs/java/micro and /quidra-benchmark/template/programs/java/adversarial: sample programs compile and run using only javac/java, no third-party jars required. | Transitive dependency resolution is delegated to external build tools (Maven/Gradle), not part of the core language; keeps runtime dependency-free but pushes complexity to tooling for larger projects. | Module system (JPMS, Java 9+) allows explicit dependency declaration via module-info.java, improving clarity over classic classpath model, but ecosystem adoption is inconsistent. | Classic classpath model can allow ambiguous or duplicate class resolution across jars (classpath hell); JPMS mitigates but does not eliminate this broadly.

component_findings.artifact_source_separation: Recertified level 4 under the current criterion: Source-level program meaning is not unnecessarily tied to a single compiler ABI, filesystem convention or host-specific build assumption. Evidence basis: language/runtime design: bytecode abstraction, standard library cross-platform APIs, opt-in native interop boundary | Java's language/runtime design (JVM bytecode target, write-once-run-anywhere) is intrinsically platform-neutral by construction: source compiles to platform-independent bytecode executed by any conformant JVM. | No platform-specific conditional compilation is required in the base language for portability; standard library APIs (java.nio.file, java.net) provide cross-platform abstractions such as Path and separator handling. | Reviewed /quidra-benchmark/template/programs/java/micro and adversarial samples: no platform-specific code, OS-conditional branches, or native-only APIs used; portable across JVM-supporting platforms by design. | Native interop (JNI/JNA/Foreign Function and Memory API) is opt-in and clearly separated from the portable core language, preserving platform neutrality of the base language while still allowing platform-specific extension when needed. | Design-level caveat: some JDK APIs and behaviors have historically differed slightly between platforms (filesystem case sensitivity, line endings, default charset behavior pre-Java 18), minor language/runtime design leaks rather than ecosystem gaps.
